ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: There are a total of 9 black dots in the figure, arranged into a 3×3 square array: three rows and three columns, with 3 dots in each row and each column. The obvious straight lines that can form 3 collinear points include 3 horizontal rows, 3 vertical columns, and 2 main diagonals. Reasoning: To make the remaining figure have no three points on the same straight line, the set of deleted points must intersect every original straight line containing 3 points. Since the three horizontal rows do not overlap with one another, each row originally has 3 collinear points, so at least 1 point must be deleted from each row. Therefore at least 3 points need to be deleted. Next prove that 3 points are sufficient: delete the 3 points on any one main diagonal, for example the upper-left, center, and lower-right three points. In this way each row has lost one point, and each column has also lost one point; this main diagonal is completely deleted, and the other main diagonal also no longer has 3 points because the center point has been deleted. Thus there are no three collinear points in the remaining figure. Final answer: 3

method.method_draft: Read the diagram as a 3 by 3 array of 9 points. The relevant 3-point straight lines include the three horizontal rows, three vertical columns, and two main diagonals. The question asks for the smallest deletion set that intersects every such 3-point line. Since the three horizontal rows are disjoint collinear triples, any valid deletion set must remove at least one point from each row, so at least 3 points are necessary. Then show 3 are sufficient by removing the three points on one main diagonal; every row, column, and diagonal is then missing at least one point, so no three remaining points are collinear. Conclude the minimum is 3.

method.method_draft: Read the picture as three horizontal rows of three points each. Instead of thinking about deleted points first, maximize how many points can remain. In any acceptable remaining picture, no row can contain all 3 of its original points, because each row is a straight line. Therefore each of the three rows can contribute at most 2 remaining points, giving at most 6 remaining points total. Since the original diagram has 9 points, at least 9 - 6 = 3 points must be removed. To verify this bound is attainable, keep the 6 points not lying on one diagonal, equivalently remove the top-left, center, and bottom-right points; then every row, column, and diagonal has at most 2 remaining points. Hence the minimum removal number is 3.
